note: Hand-curated landmarks, curiosities and moments in natural history drawn on the map. 'from'/'to' are the years the thing existed (to: null if it still stands). A drawing appears on any snapshot whose era overlaps that span. 'tier' sets when it appears: 1 from far out, 2 at regional zoom, 3 only up close. 'quip' is the caption; 'note' is the fact behind it. Dates marked approx are approximate.

drawings.name: Göbekli Tepe
drawings.quip: Monumental stonework by people who hadn't yet invented farming. Archaeologists are still recalculating.
drawings.note: Carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers around 9500 BCE, some 6,000 years before Stonehenge.

drawings.name: Stonehenge
drawings.quip: Aligned to the solstice. Purpose: still under discussion, five thousand years on.
drawings.note: The great sarsen circle was raised around 2500 BCE on a site in use since about 3000 BCE.

drawings.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
drawings.quip: Tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years. A record no skyscraper will match.
drawings.note: Built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE; the oldest of the Seven Wonders, and the only one still standing.

drawings.name: Mohenjo-daro
drawings.quip: Grid streets, covered drains, a public bath. Then, quietly, abandoned.
drawings.note: One of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, at its height around 2500 BCE.

drawings.name: Ziggurat of Ur
drawings.quip: A staircase to the moon god, in fired brick and bitumen.
drawings.note: Built around 2100 BCE by King Ur-Nammu for Nanna, the Sumerian moon god.

drawings.name: Palace of Knossos
drawings.quip: So many corridors that later Greeks told a story about a labyrinth.
drawings.note: Centre of Minoan Crete; the maze-like palace is linked to the myth of the Minotaur.

drawings.name: Abu Simbel
drawings.quip: Ramesses II, four times, sixty-five feet high. Subtlety was not the brief.
drawings.note: Carved into a cliff around 1264 BCE; moved block by block in the 1960s to escape Lake Nasser.

drawings.name: Parthenon
drawings.quip: Has almost no straight lines, by design, and has served as temple, church, mosque and gunpowder store.
drawings.note: Completed in 438 BCE for Athena; badly damaged when a Venetian shell hit the Ottoman powder store inside in 1687.

drawings.name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
drawings.quip: Gave its island's name, Pharos, to the word for lighthouse in half of Europe's languages.
drawings.note: One of the Seven Wonders, standing for over 1,500 years until earthquakes brought it down by 1323.

drawings.name: Great Stupa at Sanchi
drawings.quip: A hemisphere of brick over relics of the Buddha, commissioned by an emperor who renounced war.
drawings.note: Begun by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.

drawings.name: Great Wall of China
drawings.quip: Not visible from the Moon. Quite visible from Badaling on a Sunday.
drawings.note: Qin Shi Huang linked earlier walls after 221 BCE; most of what stands today is Ming, from after 1368.

drawings.name: Terracotta Army
drawings.quip: Eight thousand soldiers, every face different, guarding an emperor underground. Found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
drawings.note: Buried with Qin Shi Huang around 210 BCE.

drawings.name: Petra
drawings.quip: The Treasury holds no treasure. Bedouin shot at its urn for centuries checking.
drawings.note: The Nabataean rock-cut façade of Al-Khazneh dates to the early 1st century CE.

drawings.name: Colosseum
drawings.quip: Seated about 50,000. Lost much of its outer wall, largely to other people's building projects.
drawings.note: Opened in 80 CE under Titus; later quarried for stone after earthquakes damaged it.

drawings.name: Pantheon
drawings.quip: Still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. The hole in the top is deliberate.
drawings.note: Rebuilt under Hadrian around 125 CE; in continuous use ever since, as a church since 609.

drawings.name: Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan
drawings.quip: The Aztecs found it already ancient and named it 'the place where gods were born'.
drawings.note: Completed around 200 CE in what was then one of the largest cities in the world.

drawings.name: Hagia Sophia
drawings.quip: Cathedral for 900 years, mosque for nearly 500, museum for 86, mosque again since 2020.
drawings.note: Built in five years for Justinian and dedicated in 537; the minarets were added after 1453.

drawings.name: Dome of the Rock
drawings.quip: Thirteen centuries old and still one of the most contested pieces of real estate on Earth.
drawings.note: Completed in 691–692 under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik.

drawings.name: Tikal
drawings.quip: Its temples rise above the rainforest canopy. The rainforest is working on that.
drawings.note: Temple I was built around 732 CE as the tomb of the Maya king Jasaw Chan Kʼawiil I.

drawings.name: Borobudur
drawings.quip: Walk its terraces clockwise and you read 2,672 relief panels. Bring water.
drawings.note: The world's largest Buddhist monument, completed around 825 under the Shailendra dynasty.

drawings.name: Monks Mound, Cahokia
drawings.quip: Around 1100, Cahokia was about as populous as London.
drawings.note: The largest earthwork in the Americas, centre of the Mississippian culture.

drawings.name: El Castillo, Chichén Itzá
drawings.quip: At the equinox, the afternoon sun draws a serpent down the stairs. Every year, on schedule.
drawings.note: The pyramid of Kukulcán, built between the 8th and 12th centuries.

drawings.name: Tower of London
drawings.quip: Royal palace, prison, mint, zoo, and jewel box. The ravens are on the payroll.
drawings.note: William the Conqueror began the White Tower around 1078.

drawings.name: Angkor Wat
drawings.quip: Built as a Hindu temple, became a Buddhist one, and now appears on Cambodia's flag.
drawings.note: Built for King Suryavarman II in the first half of the 12th century; the largest religious monument in the world.

drawings.name: Rock churches of Lalibela
drawings.quip: Built by digging down, not building up. Each church is a single carved rock.
drawings.note: Eleven monolithic churches attributed to King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela, around 1200.

drawings.name: Great Zimbabwe
drawings.quip: Dry-stone walls eleven metres high, without a drop of mortar. A country later took its name.
drawings.note: Capital of a trading kingdom from about the 11th to the 15th century.

drawings.name: Alhambra
drawings.quip: Plain red walls outside, lace carved in plaster inside. A palace that does not show off to strangers.
drawings.note: The Nasrid palace-fortress, begun in 1238; the last Muslim stronghold in Iberia until 1492.

drawings.name: Moai of Rapa Nui
drawings.quip: Nearly a thousand of them, and they mostly face inland, keeping an eye on the islanders.
drawings.note: Carved between about 1250 and 1500, on one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth.

drawings.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
drawings.quip: Took about two centuries to build, and five years to rebuild after the 2019 fire.
drawings.note: Largely complete by 1260; reopened in December 2024.

drawings.name: Djinguereber Mosque, Timbuktu
drawings.quip: Built of mud and re-plastered by the whole town every year. The wooden spikes are the scaffolding.
drawings.note: Commissioned by Mansa Musa in 1327 after his pilgrimage to Mecca.

drawings.name: Kinkaku-ji
drawings.quip: Covered in gold leaf, burned down by a monk in 1950, rebuilt by 1955. The novel came out in 1956.
drawings.note: The Golden Pavilion, built as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu.

drawings.name: Forbidden City
drawings.quip: Home of 24 emperors. Commoners admitted from 1925, tickets now required.
drawings.note: Completed in 1420 for the Ming Yongle Emperor; the imperial palace until 1912.

drawings.name: Machu Picchu
drawings.quip: The Spanish never found it. Everyone else has.
drawings.note: An Inca estate built around 1450 for the emperor Pachacuti, abandoned a century later.

drawings.name: Moscow Kremlin
drawings.quip: The red-brick walls were designed by Italians. The word 'Kremlin' just means fortress.
drawings.note: The present walls and towers were built in 1485–1495 by Italian architects for Ivan III.

drawings.name: Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan
drawings.quip: Twin temples atop a city built on a lake. Dismantled by the Spanish, rediscovered by electricians in 1978.
drawings.note: The main temple of the Aztec capital, enlarged in seven building phases; destroyed after 1521.

drawings.name: St. Peter's Basilica
drawings.quip: Its fundraising, through the sale of indulgences, helped set off the Reformation.
drawings.note: Consecrated in 1626 after 120 years of work by Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno and others.

drawings.name: Taj Mahal
drawings.quip: A mausoleum for a beloved wife. The minarets lean outward slightly, so they would fall away from her.
drawings.note: Built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal; the mausoleum was finished around 1643.

drawings.name: Potala Palace
drawings.quip: A thousand rooms at 3,700 metres. Stairs are the main form of transport.
drawings.note: Rebuilt from 1645 under the fifth Dalai Lama; the White Palace was finished in 1648.

drawings.name: Palace of Versailles
drawings.quip: Started as a hunting lodge. Ended as the reason for a revolution, among other reasons.
drawings.note: Louis XIV moved the court here in 1682; it was the seat of royal power until 1789.

drawings.name: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben)
drawings.quip: Big Ben is the bell. The tower was renamed for a queen in 2012 and nobody calls it that.
drawings.note: Completed in 1859 as part of the rebuilt Palace of Westminster.

drawings.name: Statue of Liberty
drawings.quip: A French gift, assembled from 350 pieces. She was copper-coloured until about 1906.
drawings.note: Dedicated in 1886; designed by Bartholdi with an internal frame by Gustave Eiffel.

drawings.name: Eiffel Tower
drawings.quip: Built to stand for twenty years. Artists signed a petition against the 'useless and monstrous' thing.
drawings.note: Built for the 1889 World's Fair; the tallest structure in the world until 1930.

drawings.name: Empire State Building
drawings.quip: Built in 410 days during the Depression, then so empty it was nicknamed the 'Empty State Building'.
drawings.note: The world's tallest building from 1931 to 1970.

drawings.name: Christ the Redeemer
drawings.quip: Struck by lightning several times a year. Spare fingertips are kept for repairs.
drawings.note: Completed in 1931 on Corcovado, above Rio de Janeiro.

drawings.name: Berlin Wall
drawings.quip: Built overnight in August 1961, opened by a misread press briefing in November 1989.
drawings.note: Divided East and West Berlin for 28 years.

drawings.name: Sydney Opera House
drawings.quip: Ten years late, fourteen times over budget, and its architect never saw it finished.
drawings.note: Designed by Jørn Utzon; opened in 1973.

drawings.name: Burj Khalifa
drawings.quip: You can watch the sunset at the base, take the lift, and watch it again from the top.
drawings.note: At 828 metres, the tallest building in the world since it opened in 2010.

drawings.name: Crossing Beringia
drawings.quip: When the seas were low, you could walk from Siberia to Alaska. Some people did, and kept going.
drawings.note: The land bridge between Asia and the Americas was exposed for thousands of years during the last Ice Age.

drawings.name: The last mammoths
drawings.quip: Woolly mammoths were still alive here when the Great Pyramid was finished.
drawings.note: A small population survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.

drawings.name: Mammoth steppe
drawings.quip: The largest ecosystem on Ice Age Earth was a grassland stretching from Spain to Canada.
drawings.note: Cold, dry steppe once supported mammoths, woolly rhinos and steppe bison across northern Eurasia.

drawings.name: The dodo
drawings.quip: Unafraid of people, which turned out to be the problem. Last confirmed sighting: 1662.
drawings.note: A flightless bird found only on Mauritius, extinct within a century of Dutch sailors arriving.

drawings.name: The Trojan Horse
drawings.quip: Possibly legend, definitely the origin of 'beware of Greeks bearing gifts'.
drawings.note: Troy itself was real; the horse appears in Virgil and other sources, not in archaeology.

drawings.name: Hannibal's elephants
drawings.quip: Thirty-seven war elephants set out over the Alps. The Alps had views on this.
drawings.note: Hannibal crossed into Italy in 218 BCE; few of the elephants survived the following winter.

drawings.name: Caravan on the Silk Road
drawings.quip: Silk went west, glass and horses went east, and paper, gunpowder and plague went wherever they liked.
drawings.note: Overland routes linking China and the Mediterranean, from Han diplomacy in the 2nd century BCE.

drawings.name: Vesuvius, 79 CE
drawings.quip: Pompeii was buried in a day and preserved for 1,700 years. The graffiti survived too.
drawings.note: The eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum; Pliny the Younger's letters describe it.
drawings.wiki: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

drawings.name: Salt and gold caravan
drawings.quip: Salt from the north, gold from the south, traded at times weight for weight.
drawings.note: Camel caravans crossed the Sahara between North Africa and the Sahel kingdoms for over a thousand years.

drawings.name: Here be sea serpents
drawings.quip: Where the map ran out of facts, it ran into monsters.
drawings.note: Medieval and Renaissance maps filled unknown seas with creatures; Olaus Magnus's Carta Marina of 1539 is crowded with them.

drawings.name: Norse ship to Vinland
drawings.quip: Europeans reached America around 1000 CE, stayed a few years, and somehow didn't mention it to anyone important.
drawings.note: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is the only confirmed Norse site in the Americas.

drawings.name: Voyaging canoe
drawings.quip: Navigated by stars, swells and birds across the largest ocean on Earth. No compass required.
drawings.note: Polynesians settled Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally New Zealand between about 1000 and 1300.

drawings.name: Marco Polo at Xanadu
drawings.quip: His book was a medieval bestseller. Readers called it 'The Million', for the exaggerations.
drawings.note: Marco Polo reached Kublai Khan's summer capital, Shangdu, in 1275.

drawings.name: Mansa Musa in Cairo
drawings.quip: Spent so much gold on his way through Cairo that its value there stayed down for years.
drawings.note: The emperor of Mali passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324.

drawings.name: Zheng He's treasure fleet
drawings.quip: Seven voyages in ships far larger than Columbus's. Then the court lost interest, and the logs reportedly went missing.
drawings.note: Ming fleets reached Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa between 1405 and 1433.

drawings.name: Gutenberg's press
drawings.quip: Everything you are reading descends from a modified wine press in Mainz.
drawings.note: Movable-type printing began in Mainz around 1450; the Gutenberg Bible followed by 1455.

drawings.name: The Santa María
drawings.quip: Aiming for Japan. Off by about one Pacific Ocean.
drawings.note: Columbus's flagship crossed the Atlantic in 1492 and ran aground off Hispaniola that Christmas.

drawings.name: The Victoria
drawings.quip: First ship around the world. Five set out, one came back, and the captain was not on it.
drawings.note: Magellan's expedition left Spain in 1519; Magellan died in the Philippines, and Elcano brought Victoria home in 1522.

drawings.name: Manila galleon
drawings.quip: Mexican silver for Chinese silk, once or twice a year, for 250 years. Globalisation, by sail.
drawings.note: Spanish ships crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco from 1565 to 1815.

drawings.name: The Mayflower
drawings.quip: Bound for Virginia. Arrived in Massachusetts.
drawings.note: Carried 102 passengers across the Atlantic in 1620.

drawings.name: The Kraken
drawings.quip: Described in 1752 by a bishop. The giant squid was photographed alive in 2004.
drawings.note: Erik Pontoppidan's natural history of Norway described the kraken as a creature the size of an island.

drawings.name: Montgolfier balloon
drawings.quip: The first passengers, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. All landed fine.
drawings.note: The first crewed hot-air balloon flight followed over Paris in November 1783.

drawings.name: The golden spike
drawings.quip: Coast to coast in a week instead of six months. Legend says both dignitaries missed the spike.
drawings.note: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed at Promontory, Utah, in 1869.

drawings.name: Krakatoa
drawings.quip: Possibly the loudest sound in recorded history, heard 4,800 km away. The sunsets turned red for years.
drawings.note: The 1883 eruption destroyed most of the island and killed over 36,000 people.

drawings.name: Wright Flyer
drawings.quip: First flight: twelve seconds, 37 metres. Shorter than the wingspan of a 747.
drawings.note: The Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903.

drawings.name: RMS Titanic
drawings.quip: Carried lifeboats for about half its passengers, which was more than the law required.
drawings.note: Sank on its maiden voyage on 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg; over 1,500 died.

drawings.name: Spirit of St. Louis
drawings.quip: Thirty-three and a half hours alone over the Atlantic, with no front window. He used a periscope.
drawings.note: Charles Lindbergh flew nonstop from New York to Paris in May 1927.

drawings.name: The Hindenburg
drawings.quip: Filled with hydrogen, because the US would not sell Germany helium. It had a smoking room.
drawings.note: Destroyed by fire while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey, in May 1937.

drawings.name: Sputnik 1
drawings.quip: A polished ball the size of a beach ball, saying 'beep' to the entire planet.
drawings.note: The first artificial satellite, launched from Baikonur on 4 October 1957.

drawings.name: The first wheat
drawings.quip: Did people domesticate wheat, or did wheat domesticate people? It got the better deal.
drawings.note: Einkorn wheat was first domesticated near the Karacadağ mountains in southeastern Anatolia around 9500 BCE, one of the founding crops of farming.

drawings.name: Rice in the Yangtze valley
drawings.quip: Half the people alive today still eat it every day.
drawings.note: Rice was domesticated along the middle and lower Yangtze; cultivated rice is well established there by about 7000 BCE.

drawings.name: Maize from teosinte
drawings.quip: Bred from a wild grass with a dozen rock-hard kernels. Patience, measured in corn.
drawings.note: Maize was domesticated from teosinte in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago.

drawings.name: The Green Sahara
drawings.quip: Saharan rock art shows hippos, giraffes and people swimming. Nobody was imagining things.
drawings.note: During the African Humid Period, roughly 9000–3500 BCE, stronger monsoons turned the Sahara into grassland with lakes and rivers. The map shows it green in these eras.

drawings.name: The horse is tamed
drawings.quip: For the next four thousand years, the fastest way to get anywhere was on one of these.
drawings.note: Ancient DNA shows modern domestic horses descend from a lineage on the western Eurasian steppe around 2200 BCE, which spread across Eurasia within a few centuries.

drawings.name: Methuselah, a bristlecone pine
drawings.quip: Germinated around 2833 BCE and still alive. Its exact location is kept secret, for its own protection.
drawings.note: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California's White Mountains, among the oldest known living non-clonal trees. It appears on every map from here on.

drawings.name: The aurochs
drawings.quip: The wild ancestor of all cattle. The last one died in a Polish royal forest in 1627, royal gamekeepers notwithstanding.
drawings.note: Aurochs once ranged across Europe, Asia and North Africa, and are painted on the walls of Lascaux. The last known animal died in the Jaktorów Forest.

drawings.name: The moa
drawings.quip: Up to 3.6 metres tall with no wings at all. Gone within about two centuries of people arriving.
drawings.note: Nine species of moa lived only in New Zealand; they were hunted to extinction soon after Polynesian settlement around 1300.

drawings.name: The Columbian exchange
drawings.quip: From the Andes to Ireland in about a century. Europe's population noticed.
drawings.note: After 1492, crops, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions. Potatoes, first domesticated near Lake Titicaca, reached Spain by around 1570.

drawings.name: Tulip mania
drawings.quip: At the peak, a single bulb was said to cost as much as a canal house. Historians now think the crash was smaller than the legend.
drawings.note: A speculative bubble in contracts for tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic collapsed in February 1637.

drawings.name: Frost fair on the Thames
drawings.quip: The Little Ice Age froze the Thames hard enough for a fair. Printers on the ice sold souvenirs with your name on them.
drawings.note: During the Great Frost of 1683–84 the Thames froze for about two months; the Little Ice Age brought colder winters to Europe from roughly 1300 to 1850.

drawings.name: Tambora and the year without a summer
drawings.quip: The largest eruption in recorded history cooled the planet. In the cold, wet summer that followed, Mary Shelley began Frankenstein.
drawings.note: Mount Tambora erupted in April 1815; crop failures across the Northern Hemisphere made 1816 'the year without a summer'.

drawings.name: The passenger pigeon
drawings.quip: Once perhaps the most numerous bird on Earth, in flocks that took hours to pass. The last one, Martha, died in Cincinnati in 1914.
drawings.note: Market hunting and forest clearance took passenger pigeons from billions to none in about a century.

drawings.name: The Dust Bowl
drawings.quip: On Black Sunday, 14 April 1935, the dust turned day into night and gave the disaster its name.
drawings.note: Drought and ploughed-up prairie grassland blew away the topsoil of the southern Great Plains, driving hundreds of thousands of people west.

drawings.name: The thylacine
drawings.quip: The last known Tasmanian tiger died in a Hobart zoo in 1936, two months after the species was given legal protection.
drawings.note: A striped marsupial predator, hunted to extinction under government bounties.

drawings.name: Wolves of Chernobyl
drawings.quip: People left in 1986. Wolves, lynx, bison and wild horses moved in.
drawings.note: The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, evacuated after the 1986 reactor disaster, has become an unplanned wildlife refuge.

drawings.name: Persepolis
drawings.quip: A ceremonial capital for the King of Kings. Alexander burned it in 330 BCE, possibly after a long night.
drawings.note: Begun by Darius I around 518 BCE; its stairways are carved with delegations from across the Persian Empire bringing tribute.

drawings.name: Ishtar Gate, Babylon
drawings.quip: Glazed blue bricks, lions and dragons. Most of it now stands in a museum in Berlin.
drawings.note: Built by Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BCE as the eighth gate of Babylon; reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum from excavated bricks.

drawings.name: Pont du Gard
drawings.quip: Fifty kilometres of aqueduct dropping just 12 metres along its whole length. Roman surveyors did not round up.
drawings.note: A Roman aqueduct bridge carrying water to Nîmes, built in the 1st century CE.

drawings.name: Hadrian's Wall
drawings.quip: Built to mark where Rome ended. Letters from soldiers stationed nearby ask home for socks.
drawings.note: Begun in 122 CE across northern Britain. Tablets from the fort at Vindolanda preserve soldiers' letters, including one about sending socks.

drawings.name: Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba
drawings.quip: A forest of 856 columns, with a cathedral built in the middle in the 1500s. The emperor who approved it is said to have regretted it.
drawings.note: Begun in 785 under Abd al-Rahman I; its red-and-white double arches are among the great sights of Islamic architecture.

drawings.name: Shwedagon Pagoda
drawings.quip: Gilded from top to bottom and crowned with thousands of diamonds; the topmost alone is 76 carats.
drawings.note: Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site, probably first built between the 6th and 10th centuries and enlarged many times since.

drawings.name: Mont-Saint-Michel
drawings.quip: Cut off by the tide twice a day, which is how it held out through the Hundred Years' War.
drawings.note: A tidal island abbey off Normandy; the Romanesque abbey church was begun in 1023.

drawings.name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
drawings.quip: Began leaning during construction, in 1178. They carried on building it anyway, for two centuries.
drawings.note: The bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, built in stages from 1173 to 1372 on soft ground.

drawings.name: St Basil's Cathedral
drawings.quip: Legend says Ivan the Terrible blinded its architects so they could never build anything finer. Probably untrue.
drawings.note: Built 1555–1561 on Red Square to commemorate the capture of Kazan.

drawings.name: Great Mosque of Djenné
drawings.quip: The largest mud-brick building in the world. Each spring the whole town turns out to re-plaster it.
drawings.note: The present building dates from 1907, on the site of a 13th-century mosque.

drawings.name: Sagrada Família
drawings.quip: Under construction since 1882. Gaudí, on the delay: 'My client is not in a hurry.'
drawings.note: Antoni Gaudí's basilica in Barcelona, still being completed more than a century after his death.

drawings.name: Neuschwanstein
drawings.quip: Built by a reclusive king as a private retreat. It opened to paying visitors seven weeks after he died.
drawings.note: Ludwig II of Bavaria's fairy-tale castle, begun in 1869 and never finished.

drawings.name: Tower Bridge
drawings.quip: Still lifts for ships hundreds of times a year. In 1952 a double-decker bus jumped the opening gap.
drawings.note: A combined bascule and suspension bridge over the Thames, opened in 1894.

drawings.name: Golden Gate Bridge
drawings.quip: Painted 'International Orange' to stand out in fog. The US Navy had wanted black and yellow stripes.
drawings.note: Opened in 1937; the longest suspension span in the world until 1964.

drawings.name: Lascaux cave paintings
drawings.quip: Painted by firelight about 17,000 years ago. Rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers following their dog.
drawings.note: Hundreds of animals, including aurochs, horses and deer, painted deep inside a cave in southwestern France.

drawings.name: Doggerland
drawings.quip: Britain was once attached to Europe by a plain of rivers and marshes. Then the sea came in.
drawings.note: Rising seas after the last Ice Age drowned this land between Britain and the continent by about 6200 BCE.

drawings.name: Ötzi the Iceman
drawings.quip: Died about 5,300 years ago with an arrowhead in his shoulder. The hikers who found him in 1991 assumed a recent accident.
drawings.note: A naturally mummified man found in the Ötztal Alps, with his copper axe, bow, clothing and 61 tattoos.

drawings.name: Nok terracottas
drawings.quip: West Africa's oldest known figurative sculptures, with remarkably elaborate hairstyles.
drawings.note: Terracotta heads and figures made by the Nok culture of central Nigeria from about 500 BCE.

drawings.name: Nazca Lines
drawings.quip: A hummingbird 90 metres long, best appreciated from an aircraft its makers never had.
drawings.note: Hundreds of lines and figures scraped into the Peruvian desert by the Nazca culture.

drawings.name: Antikythera mechanism
drawings.quip: A bronze computer of some 30 gears for predicting eclipses. Nothing as intricate survives for another thousand years.
drawings.note: Recovered in 1901 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the island of Antikythera.

drawings.name: Ajanta Caves
drawings.quip: Painted Buddhist halls, abandoned to the jungle until a British tiger-hunting party stumbled in in 1819.
drawings.note: Rock-cut monasteries with some of the finest surviving ancient Indian paintings.

drawings.name: The Library Cave at Dunhuang
drawings.quip: Sealed around 1000 CE with tens of thousands of manuscripts, including the oldest dated printed book.
drawings.note: The Diamond Sutra found here is dated 868; the cave was rediscovered in 1900.

drawings.name: The magnetic compass
drawings.quip: Chinese navigators were steering by compass by about 1100. Europe caught up a century or so later.
drawings.note: Song-dynasty writers describe magnetised needles for finding direction in the 11th century.

drawings.name: The Bayeux Tapestry
drawings.quip: Actually an embroidery, 70 metres long, featuring Halley's Comet and a great many horses.
drawings.note: Tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

drawings.name: The Mongol relay riders
drawings.quip: Changing horses at stations along the way, a messenger could cover around 200 km a day.
drawings.note: The Yam, a network of relay stations across the Mongol Empire, carried orders, officials and merchants.

drawings.name: The Mona Lisa
drawings.quip: Commissioned by a Florentine silk merchant, who never got it. Leonardo kept it with him for the rest of his life.
drawings.note: Begun around 1503; it travelled with Leonardo to France, where he died in 1519.

drawings.name: The first coffeehouses
drawings.quip: Istanbul's coffeehouses opened in 1554. Authorities kept trying to shut them as dens of gossip and sedition.
drawings.note: Coffee drinking spread from Yemen through the Ottoman world, and from there to Europe in the 1600s.

drawings.name: The Globe Theatre
drawings.quip: Burned down in 1613 when a stage cannon set the thatched roof alight during a performance of Henry VIII.
drawings.note: Built in 1599 by Shakespeare's company; many of his plays premiered here.

drawings.name: Galileo's telescope
drawings.quip: Pointed at Jupiter in January 1610, it found four moons and a good deal of trouble.
drawings.note: Galileo's observations from Padua supported the Copernican view that the Earth goes round the Sun.

drawings.name: Newton's apple tree
drawings.quip: Plague closed Cambridge, so Newton went home to Lincolnshire and worked out gravity and calculus. The tree is still alive.
drawings.note: Newton later told the story of the falling apple at Woolsthorpe Manor in 1666.

drawings.name: The pirates' republic
drawings.quip: For a dozen years Nassau was run by pirates. Blackbeard was one of its citizens.
drawings.note: The Republic of Pirates ended when Woodes Rogers arrived as royal governor in 1718.

drawings.name: HMS Endeavour
drawings.quip: Charted the east coast of Australia in 1770, then ran aground on the Great Barrier Reef.
drawings.note: James Cook's first voyage of exploration, 1768–1771.

drawings.name: HMS Beagle in the Galápagos
drawings.quip: Darwin spent five weeks here and only realised how much the finches mattered after he got home.
drawings.note: The Galápagos visit in 1835 fed into Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, published in 1859.

drawings.name: The California gold rush
drawings.quip: San Francisco went from about 1,000 people to 25,000 in a single year.
drawings.note: Gold found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848 drew some 300,000 people to California.

drawings.name: The transatlantic cable
drawings.quip: The 1858 cable worked for three weeks. Queen Victoria's 98-word greeting took about 16 hours to send.
drawings.note: A lasting cable was laid in 1866 by the Great Eastern, then the largest ship ever built.

drawings.name: The Panama Canal
drawings.quip: Ships from New York to San Francisco no longer had to go round South America: some 13,000 km saved.
drawings.note: Opened in August 1914, less than three weeks after the First World War began.

drawings.name: Penicillin
drawings.quip: Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to find mould killing the bacteria on a dish he'd left out.
drawings.note: Discovered in 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London; mass-produced from the 1940s.

drawings.name: Amelia Earhart's last flight
drawings.quip: Vanished near tiny Howland Island in July 1937, with about 11,000 km of her round-the-world flight still to go.
drawings.note: Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan were never found.

drawings.name: The Kon-Tiki
drawings.quip: A balsa raft from Peru to Polynesia in 101 days, to prove it could be done. It could.
drawings.note: Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 expedition; DNA studies later showed some early Polynesian–South American contact.

drawings.name: The World Wide Web
drawings.quip: Tim Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal came back from his boss marked 'vague but exciting'.
drawings.note: Invented at CERN; the first website went online in 1991. The printing press of its day.

drawings.name: The Great Wave
drawings.quip: Hokusai made it in his seventies and said he hoped to have mastered drawing by the age of 110.
drawings.note: The Great Wave off Kanagawa, a woodblock print from his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.

drawings.name: The Laki eruption
drawings.quip: Its fumes darkened skies across Europe and ruined harvests. Some historians see a link to the French Revolution.
drawings.note: The eight-month fissure eruption killed about a fifth of Iceland's people, mostly through famine.

drawings.name: Horses return to the Americas
drawings.quip: Horses had died out in the Americas over 10,000 years before. The Spanish brought them back; the Comanche made the most of it.
drawings.note: Within two centuries, horses transformed the lives of the Plains peoples.

drawings.name: The cattle plague
drawings.quip: Swept Africa in the 1890s, killing up to nine in ten cattle. In 2011 it became only the second disease ever eradicated.
drawings.note: Rinderpest's arrival caused famine across East and southern Africa.

drawings.name: Yellowstone
drawings.quip: The world's first national park, created in 1872 while bison elsewhere were being shot by the million.
drawings.note: Fewer than a thousand plains bison remained by the late 1880s; Yellowstone sheltered one of the last wild herds.

drawings.name: The Great Barrier Reef
drawings.quip: The largest structure built by living things, mostly by animals smaller than a grain of rice.
drawings.note: Over 2,300 km of coral reefs; its present form grew after sea levels rose at the end of the last Ice Age.

drawings.name: Antarctica sighted
drawings.quip: No human saw Antarctica until 1820. The penguins had not been waiting.
drawings.note: Russian, British and American expeditions all sighted the continent or its coasts in 1820.

drawings.name: Steller's sea cow
drawings.quip: Discovered in 1741: a nine-metre relative of the manatee. Hunted to extinction by 1768.
drawings.note: Known only from the Commander Islands in the Bering Sea, described by the naturalist Georg Steller.

drawings.name: The great auk
drawings.quip: The original 'penguin', before the name moved south. The last known pair was killed off Iceland in 1844.
drawings.note: A flightless North Atlantic seabird hunted for feathers, meat and oil.
